v.why: With edge 4 absent, a conv on the direct input-to-output edge adds a much-needed path and capacity to node 3, giving positive gains (exps 6-10) versus negative changes when edge 4 already carries a conv (exps 1-5).
When edge 5 is none the output node is starved of inputs, so adding a conv on edge 3 helps far more (exp 6 huge gain, exp 1 near-neutral versus negative for other edge-5 ops).
Removing edge 3 when edge 4 is also absent leaves node 3 with at most one input or none at all, causing large accuracy drops (exps 21, 22, 27, 29).
If edge 5 is none, deleting edge 3 can disconnect the output entirely or leave a single weak path, producing catastrophic losses (exps 21, 23, 29).
Replacing none with skip adds a new path from node 2 to the output (exps 45, 50 large gains), whereas replacing a conv with skip removes capacity (exps 43, 46, 47, 49).
Swapping a 3x3 conv on the final edge for an identity loses learnable capacity, consistently hurting all three datasets (exps 43, 47, 49).
Adding a residual input-to-output connection where none existed improves gradient flow and connectivity (exps 81, 85) far more than replacing an existing op on edge 3.
Without the direct edge 3 path, a conv on edge 4 is critical for reaching the output (exp 91 huge, exp 92 solid) compared with small gains when edge 3 already has a conv (exps 93, 94).
With edge 1 absent, node 2 receives little or no signal, so upgrading edge 5 has small or negative effect (exps 11, 12) versus large gains when edge 1 feeds node 2 (exps 13-18).

When edge 2 is none, node 1 feeds the output only through edge 4 (often absent), so strengthening edge 0 brings little or negative change (exps 31, 32) versus consistent gains when edge 2 is active (exps 33-37).

raw:
I grouped the 100 experiments by edit and looked for parent features that consistently change an edit's sign or size across all three datasets. Most of the strong interactions come from connectivity. Node 3 is reached only through edges 3, 4 and 5, and a node with no live incoming path contributes nothing. So the same edit can either change a working network slightly or decide whether the network functions at all.

The hypotheses with the clearest support:
- **Reconnecting the output (hypotheses 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8).** Adding an op on edge 3, 4 or 5 gains a lot when it replaces `none` or when the other output edges are absent (experiments 6, 45, 50, 81, 85, 91, 93).
- **Removing edge 3 (hypotheses 2, 3).** Setting it to `none` is catastrophic when it is the only surviving input to node 3 (experiments 21, 29).
- **Dead intermediate nodes (hypotheses 9, 10).** An edit on an edge out of node 1 or node 2 barely matters when that node has no route to the output (experiments 11–12 and 31–32).

**Caveat:** some of these rest on few matching parents. The hypotheses keyed on edge 4 = `none` or edge 5 = `none` are partly driven by single disconnected-cell outliers, so their consistent margin is less certain than the size of those outliers suggests.
